faqs.answer: A bundt pan has a center tube, so it has no flat floor to measure. Area maths needs a floor. Volume is the honest comparison for any pan with a tube, and it is how bundt pans are sold: by their cup capacity.
faqs.question: Why volume and not area for a bundt?

faqs.answer: Yes. Pour the bundt batter straight into the 9x13 and the cake bakes thinner, about 2 inches deep instead of 3. Check it 10 to 15 minutes early. Scale it only when you want the sheet cake to have real height.
faqs.question: Can I use the same batter without scaling?

faqs.answer: Yes. The batter is the same batter, and butter cakes and pound cakes bake well flat. Pour any glaze over the top in the pan and it soaks in nicely. Sponge and angel food cakes do not suit the swap, because they need the tube to climb.
faqs.question: Does a bundt recipe work as a sheet cake?

formula.text: New batter = recipe batter x 1.4. Factor = new volume divided by old volume = 14 divided by 10 = 1.4.

howToSteps.name: Work out the factor
howToSteps.text: A 9x13 holds 14 cups and a standard bundt holds 10. Divide 14 by 10 and the factor is 1.4. This swap uses volume, because the bundt tube has no floor area to measure.

howToSteps.name: Scale every ingredient
howToSteps.text: Multiply each ingredient by 1.4, including the leavening. A recipe with 6 cups of batter becomes 8.4 cups.

howToSteps.name: Check the fill
howToSteps.text: Pour the scaled batter into a greased 9x13 pan. It should sit no higher than two-thirds full, about 9.3 cups. Bake any extra separately.

howToSteps.name: Bake at the same temperature, check early
howToSteps.text: Keep the oven temperature the recipe gives, but start checking 10 to 15 minutes before the bundt bake time. The shallower batter sets faster.

lede: A 10-cup bundt pan and a 9x13 pan hold different amounts, so this swap runs on volume, not area: 14 cups divided by 10 cups is 1.4. The shallower batter in the 9x13 bakes faster, so start checking 10 to 15 minutes early.

title: Bundt Pan to 9x13 Pan Converter
tutorial: A bundt pan has a hole in the middle, and that hole breaks the area maths. There is no floor to measure, because the center tube takes the middle of the pan and carries heat into it. So this swap runs on volume instead: a standard bundt pan holds 10 cups, a 9x13 holds 14 cups to the rim, and 14 divided by 10 is 1.4.

A typical bundt recipe makes about 6 cups of batter, which is also about what a 9x13 cake makes. Scaled by 1.4, 6 cups becomes 8.4 cups in the 9x13. That sits under the two-thirds fill line for a 9x13, which is about 9.3 cups. One honest note on the 14-cup figure: straight-wall geometry says a 9x13 holds 16.2 cups, but pans taper toward the base, and the measured capacity bakers use is 14 cups. This converter uses the measured figure.

The bake time changes here, because the depth changes. A bundt pan is about 3.5 inches deep and the tube carries heat to the center, so a bundt bakes long and slow, usually 50 to 60 minutes. In a 9x13 the same batter sits about 2 inches deep with no tube, and it bakes faster. A bundt takes about 30 percent longer than a 9x13 for the same batter, so start checking the sheet cake 10 to 15 minutes before the bundt time.

Do not pour the full scaled batter in without checking the fill. A bundt recipe that makes 7 cups becomes 9.8 cups scaled, which is past two-thirds of the 9x13. Bake the extra in a ramekin or a small loaf pan rather than overfilling the sheet pan. An overfull 9x13 domes in the middle and the center stays wet while the edges dry out.

The cake that comes out is the same cake, just flatter. A bundt glaze poured over the top becomes a sheet-cake topping, and it soaks in a little more on the flat top, which is no bad thing. What you lose is the bundt shape and its crusty ridges. What you gain is a cake that slices into neat squares and fits in a container.
